Geophys. J. fnt. (1993) 115, 97-108
Rock magnetic and magnetic fabric variations across three thin
alkaline dykes from Sunnhordland, Western Norway; influence of
initial mineralogy and secondary chemical alterations
Harald Walderhaug
Institute of Solid Earth Physics, Alligt. 41, 5007 Bergen, Norway
Accepted 1993 February 10. Received 1993 February 9; in original form 1992 May 12
SUMMARY
Profiles of natural remanent magnetization (NRM), rock magnetic properties and
anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) across three thin (26 to 109 cm) alkaline
dykes from Sunnhordland, Western Norway are presented.
The magnetic remanence is carried by pseudo-single-domain (PSD) low-
temperature oxidized titanomagnetite, with circa 6 per cent of cations substituted by
aluminium. Systematic variations in magnetic properties across the dykes are caused
by differences in titanomagnetite concentration as well as grain size. Low-
temperature alteration and laboratory oxidation by heating in air to a maximum
temperature of 600 "C,d o not homogenize the magnetic properties across the dykes.
Fine-grained regions near dyke margins carry the most stable remanent magnetiza-
tion, but are also most amenable to secondary chemical remanent magnetization
(CRM) resetting.
Between dyke variations in magnetic properties are larger than within dyke
variations. A stable primary remanence is found in two of the dykes, while the
third is totally reset by a soft viscous remanent magnetization (VRM), despite
similar optical grain sizes, magnetic mineralogy and oxidation state. The difference
is attributed to a lower titanium content in the latter dyke, preventing effective
partitioning of magnetic grains during low-temperature alteration.
Laboratory heating affects anisotropy variations across the dykes, resulting in
more consistent axis orientations within each dyke, and symmetric edge-to-edge
variations in the degree of anisotropy. AMS directions are different from those in
the country rock, and vary systematically across the thinnest dyke before heating.
Key words: dykes, magnetic fabric, palaeomagnetism, rock magnetism.

has taken place in all three dykes, accounting for the high
observed Curie points. This would lead to a significant
reduction in effective magnetic grain size in the two thinner
dykes, which have Fe/Ti ratios comparable to sea-floor
basalts, leaving stable magnetic carriers of PSD size. Only
half this amount of titanium is present in TM grains in the
ST dyke, leading to less secondary partitioning, and leaving
larger iron-enriched regions closer to the MD-size range.
\
The fine-grained zones near dyke margins carry the most
stable remanence, but are at the same time more vulnerable
to secondary CRM resetting (Halls 1991). A large
surface-to-volume ratio in magnetic grains, combined with
easier access of water and oxygen due to marginal cracks,
may lead to a higher oxidation state, as observed in the ST
Oblate
dyke. Moderate single-phase oxidation of small TM grains
704 Y R does not change remanence directions, but if oxidation
proceeds too far, with formation of new rhombohedra1
magnetic phases, directional resetting will occur (Dunlop
::I 1990).
;i ,I Formation of secondary magnetic minerals from non-
magnetic matrix material is also most likely to occur near
I I ProlatI e dyke margins, and will have a relatively larger impact on
0 bulk magnetic properties due to the lower concentration of
0 5 10 15 20 25 magnetic material. This is demonstrated by the relative
cm

1.6 7 SA -Grains near dyke edges carry the most stable remanent
magnetization due to smaller initial grains sizes, but are also
most vulnerable to secondary low-temperature oxidation
and CRM overprinting.
-Despite roughly similar optical grain size and magnetic
mineralogy, between dyke variations in remanent stability
are larger than within dyke variations, with a soft, unstable
VRM parallel to the present-day field in the broadest dyke
and a stable remanence in the two thinner dykes. This is
d
attributed to a lower initial titanium content in the TM
0.0 5 10 15 20 25 phases of the broadest dyke, which impedes magnetic
partitioning of the grains during oxidation.
2.0 -AMS directions in the dykes differ from those in the
country rock. Anisotropy increases towards dyke edges, and
0
CV 1.6 shows a simpler pattern after heating in all three dykes. This
x
is attributed to the removal of overprinted contributions due
\ 1.2 to low-temperature oxidation and tectonic stress, leaving a
'primary' AMS, which may reflect initial crystal growth and
0-
